title: Observation of Non-linear hall effect in Polycrystalline magnetic multilayes
authors: Preet Kamal, Chirag kalouni, Amiya Mondal, Awadesh Narayan, Debangsu Roy
abstract: The Nonlinear Hall effect(NLHE) driven principally by the Berry curvature dipole has been established in non-centrosymmetric vander Waals crystals, topological semimetals, and moiré superlattices, but its extension to technologically mature heavy-metal/ferromagnet multilayer platforms remains largely unexplored. Here, we report the observation of a robust NLHE in polycrystalline magnetic multilayers, persisting from 2 K to room temperature. The second-harmonic transverse voltage is independent of both excitation frequency and applied out-of-plane magnetic field, while the vanishingly small third-harmonic response confirms that the observed signal is not dominated by a quantum-metric contribution and instead reflects a genuine second-order electronic response. A scaling analysis of the second-order Hall conductivity against the longitudinal conductivity identifies a dominant, conductivity-independent term establishing the intrinsic berry curvature dipole. Our theoretical analysis, supported by first-principles DFT calculations, further satisfies and corroborates the experimental results. These results establish sputter-deposited polycrystalline thin film as the first engineered magnetic multilayer platform for BCD-driven nonlinear Hall transport, extending the NLHE material landscape beyond van der Waals systems into scalable, industry-compatible thin-film spintronic architectures suitable for high frequency rectifications and nonlinear sensors.
summary: This work reports the observation of a robust Nonlinear Hall effect in polycrystalline magnetic multilayers, establishing them as a new platform for studying BCD-driven transport. By analyzing second-harmonic signals and confirming symmetry constraints via DFT, the authors prove that the NLHE arises from intrinsic electronic band structure asymmetry rather than extrinsic or quantum-metric effects.
main_problem: The study aims to observe and characterize the Nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) driven by the Berry curvature dipole (BCD) in technologically relevant magnetic multilayer platforms, extending beyond traditional van der Waals systems.
main_result: A robust NLHE was observed in polycrystalline magnetic multilayers persisting up to room temperature, confirming that the signal originates from an intrinsic BCD mechanism rather than quantum-metric contributions.
method: The research combines transport measurements (measuring second-harmonic transverse voltage) with theoretical analysis using symmetry principles and first-principles DFT calculations.
model_or_system: The physical system is a sputter-deposited polycrystalline magnetic multilayer heterostructure, specifically Ta/Pt/[Ir/Fe/Co/Pt]n/Pt on Si/SiO2. The theory models the NLHE via the Berry curvature dipole (BCD) mechanism in systems lacking inversion symmetry.
key_observables: Second-harmonic transverse voltage ($V_{xy}^{2\omega}$), second-order Hall conductivity, and the temperature dependence of resistance ($R_{xx}$).
important_parameters: Temperature range (2 K to room temperature); applied magnetic field strength ($\pm 2 	ext{ T}$); excitation frequency.
main_assumptions: The observed signal is assumed to be dominated by the intrinsic BCD mechanism, and the polycrystalline structure's texture dictates the symmetry constraints on the response.
figures_summary: Figures show layer architecture, Hall bar geometry, $R_{xx}$ vs. temperature (metallic behavior), XRD patterns confirming polycrystalline growth, and plots of $V_{xy}^{2\omega}$ dependence on current, frequency, and magnetic field.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the experimental observation of NLHE in multilayers, rigorously rules out other sources (frequency/field independence, no third harmonic), uses scaling analysis to isolate the BCD term, and finally supports these findings with DFT calculations that confirm the necessary symmetry breaking for a nonzero BCD moment.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter physics, the study of nonlinear transport phenomena in engineered interfaces touches upon non-equilibrium quantum dynamics. The precise identification of an intrinsic electronic mechanism (BCD) provides a model for understanding how broken symmetries dictate macroscopic electrical responses in solid-state devices.
